doc.title: Bill Berry and Buster Cooper interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995

chapter: Statesmen and the world of jazz
title: Race prejudice and jazz education; Berry at Berklee
summary: Berry blames prejudice for jazz's low standing and recalls studying at the new Berklee.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Well the way they say that is that because Europe is so much older than America, they have that continuity of being appreciative of art. I mean they’ve had art for a thousand years instead of two hundred, or one hundred in the case of jazz. Plus I think one of the reasons jazz is not well liked here in this country is strictly race prejudice you know. And always was, right from the beginning. And when I was in college, there was no jazz being taught in any schools. In high school —
That was taboo so to speak.

I went to Berklee when it was brand new. It was a little, tiny, you know, just about three or four rooms that’s all it was. And it was the only school in the country that I knew of that was teaching jazz at that time. Now it’s you know, all over the country. In fact I’ve done a lot of things with kids in Japan and in Europe too. Student jazz musicians.
